study.title: Mark 12 Conflicts in the temple, central commandments, and the value of total surrender
study.overview: Mark 12 shows Jesus teaching and being confronted in the temple. First, he tells a parable against the religious leaders, showing that God expects the fruit of those who have received spiritual privileges and who reject the Son brings judgment. Then Jesus responds to traps about taxes and resurrection with wisdom that exposes hypocrisy and corrects doctrinal error. Then he summarizes God's will in the integral love of God and neighbor. Finally, Jesus denounces the vanity and exploitation of the scribes and praises a poor widow whose offering reveals confidence and total devotion.

outline.title: The Parable of the Vineyard and the Rejection of the Son
outline.explanation: Jesus tells the story of a owner who entrusts his vineyard to farmers, but they mistreat the servants and kill his son. The parable accuses the religious leaders and announces that God will judge their infidelity and grant the vineyard to others. The quotation from the rejected stone shows that human rejection does not prevent God's purpose.

outline.title: Tribute to Caesar and the responsibility before God
outline.explanation: Pharisees and herodianos try to arrest Jesus in a political response. He exposes their hypocrisy and states that Caesar must be given what belongs to him, without stealing from God what is his. The answer avoids the trap and sets the absolute priority of God.

outline.title: Resurrection, commandment greater and closeness of the Kingdom
outline.explanation: The Sadducees deny the resurrection, but Jesus shows that they err because they do not know the Scriptures or the power of God. Then, in responding to the scribe, he unites exclusive love for God and love of neighbor as the heart of the law. The scribe recognizes this, and Jesus declares that he is not far from the Kingdom of God.

outline.title: Christ greater than David and the widow who gives everything
outline.explanation: Jesus questions the limited reading of the scribes about the Messiah as the son of David and shows that the Christ is also Lord of David. Then warn against the ostentation and religious injustice of the scribes. The chapter ends with the offering of the poor widow, who gives of her sustenance and is presented by Jesus as an example superior to that of the abundant donations of the rich.

study.context: According to the notes provided, these events occur in the temple, in the context of increasing opposition to Jesus. The parable of the vineyard echoes Isaiah, where the vineyard symbolizes the people of God, and the controversy about tribute, resurrection and commandments reflects real religious debates among influential groups. The notes also indicate that people's offer was deposited in a public treasure in the temple, linked to practices of piety and charity.
study.theology: The chapter emphasizes God's faithfulness to human infidelity. The parable teaches that spiritual privileges require fruit, and reject God's servants culminates in rejecting the Son, which brings judgment. The answer about tribute shows that civil authority is real, but not absolute; the image and inscription of the coin point to the distinction between earthly duties and total belonging to God. In the discussion with the Sadducees, Jesus affirms the resurrection as biblical truth and reveals that God is God of the living, not of the dead. At the center of everything, the greatest commandment unites total love for God and love of neighbor, showing that true obedience is not an empty ritual, but surrender of the heart. The poor widow illustrates this surrender: she not only offers a small amount, but all her sustenance, and Jesus treats her as an example of what it means to fully trust in God.

scholarViews.insight: The widow's offering is presented as a radical contrast to the logic of the world: Jesus and the Father look at the heart, and the woman did exactly what Jesus had been teaching about following with full surrender.
The parable of the vineyard depicts the sin and ruin of the unfaithful Jewish community, showing that God expected the fruit of those who received their privileges.
Jesus was teaching in the temple when he questioned the understanding of the scribes about the Christ; the point is that the Messiah is not only the son of David, for David calls him Lord.

questions: What kind of fruit does God expect of whom he has received his word, his gifts and his spiritual responsibility?
In which areas can I be giving Caesar what is Caesar's, but retaining from God what belongs to him completely?
Does my devotion to God appear more in religious appearance or in practical, generous and sacrificial love?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to integrity. Examine whether your faith bears fruit, whether your doctrine is subject to Scripture and if your love for God is total and visible in dealing with people. Practice an offering of yourself: time, resources, attention, and obedience. Avoid religiosity of appearance and seek a life in which what you give God is more precious than what is left.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are incomplete in some points and some sentences have been truncated; therefore, the study avoids historical details or explanations not explicitly backed by them. It was also not possible to assign to each commentator more than one point, because the instruction requires exactly one per source.
